outline.chapter_title: 1. Case Overview, Facts, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the prosecution of Justin Cutbank, the factual events leading to the firearm charge, and the procedural path from trial through appeal. It frames how the underlying domestic violence incident, Cutbank’s later confrontation with police, and the recovery of the sawed-off rifle set up both the conviction and the sentencing disputes reviewed by the Eighth Circuit.
subtopics: The charged offense: felon in possession under 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(e)
The November 19–20, 2020 events at D.F.’s home: methamphetamine use, threats, confinement, and assault with a gun
Witnesses present in the home: D.F., her children, and housemate C.F.
Cutbank’s flight from the home and the second incident at a nearby garage
The police response: barricade, erratic statements, claimed possession of a weapon, and resistance to arrest
Physical evidence recovered along the likely route: cell phone, knife, and sawed-off Marlin .22 rifle
DNA and witness identification linking Cutbank to the firearm
Jury findings: guilt on the firearm charge and finding of three prior violent felonies for ACCA purposes
Sentence imposed: 292 months within the advisory Guidelines range
Issues on appeal: multiple evidentiary/procedural objections and challenge to the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement

outline.chapter_title: 2. Prior Possession Evidence and the Line Between Intrinsic Proof and Rule 404(b)
outline.description: This chapter explains the court’s treatment of testimony that D.F. and C.F. had seen Cutbank with the same sawed-off rifle before the charged night. It focuses on why the court characterized the testimony as intrinsic evidence of possession rather than prohibited propensity evidence under Rule 404(b), and why that distinction mattered to proving the felon-in-possession charge.
subtopics: Cutbank’s pretrial motion to exclude testimony about earlier sightings of the rifle
The defense theory: prior sightings as improper propensity evidence under Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b)
The government’s theory: intrinsic evidence showing ownership, control, and continuous possession of the same weapon
The district court’s ruling allowing D.F. and C.F. to testify about prior observations
The Eighth Circuit’s reliance on United States v. Battle: prior possession of the same firearm as directly relevant to later possession
How the testimony helped prove knowing possession of the recovered sawed-off rifle
The appellate court’s treatment of Cutbank’s failure to meaningfully challenge the district court’s reasoning
Why the court saw no evidentiary error in admitting the prior-possession testimony

outline.chapter_title: 3. Trial Management, Hearsay, Cross-Examination, and Evidentiary Discretion
outline.description: This chapter collects the remaining trial-level evidentiary and procedural disputes. It shows how the Eighth Circuit evaluated the district court’s handling of requested limiting instructions, hearsay and Confrontation Clause concerns, testimony explaining prior inconsistent statements, and restrictions on impeachment through a police report. The chapter emphasizes standards of review and the trial court’s broad discretion over evidence.
subtopics: Cutbank’s request for a limiting instruction concerning D.F.’s statements to police before she testified
The government’s position that officers would testify for context and not for inadmissible hearsay purposes
Standard of review for refusal to give a limiting instruction: abuse of discretion
Why the court found no hearsay problem on the record
Why the Confrontation Clause was satisfied once D.F. testified in person at trial
D.F.’s cross-examination about prior inconsistent statements concerning the gun
Her explanation that she was unfamiliar with guns and disliked them because her sister had been killed by a gun
The motion to strike that testimony and the Rule 403 prejudice analysis
C.F.’s similar mention of D.F.’s sister and the absence of a defense objection
The defense effort to impeach C.F. with prior statements made to a police investigator
The district court’s requirement that the police report be properly authenticated before its contents could be read into the record
Use of extrinsic impeachment evidence and the authentication requirement under United States v. Cumbie
The appellate court’s criticism of the government for unnecessarily broadening the issues on appeal
The broader principle that trial judges have substantial leeway in controlling the admission and use of evidence

outline.chapter_title: 4. Harmless Error, Cumulative Error, and Why the Conviction Was Affirmed
outline.description: This chapter explains why none of the asserted evidentiary or procedural problems justified reversal even if any ruling had been imperfect. It focuses on the harmless-error framework, the cumulative-error argument, and the strength of the government’s proof, showing how appellate courts often resolve a cluster of trial objections by asking whether the verdict was likely affected.
subtopics: The harmless-error standard for evidentiary rulings in criminal cases
The requirement that the defendant show the jury may have been substantially swayed by the challenged evidence
The court’s view that the government’s case was substantial both physically and testimonialy
Key evidence supporting conviction: D.F.’s account, C.F.’s identification, recovered firearm, and DNA match
Why any alleged evidentiary missteps would have had at most a slight influence on the verdict
The cumulative-error doctrine and its requirement of substantial prejudice
The Eighth Circuit’s conclusion that Cutbank failed to show prejudice from the combined effect of the challenged rulings
How this analysis independently supports affirmance of the conviction

outline.chapter_title: 5. Sentencing Under ACCA and the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancement
outline.description: This chapter addresses the sentencing appeal. It explains the interaction between the Armed Career Criminal Act, the Presentence Investigation Report, and the Guidelines calculations, then analyzes why the Eighth Circuit rejected Cutbank’s challenge to the four-level enhancement for possessing the firearm in connection with another felony offense. It also distinguishes procedural correctness in calculating the Guidelines from the separate question of substantive reasonableness under § 3553(a).
subtopics: The jury’s ACCA-related finding of at least three prior violent felonies
The PSR’s offense-level calculation: base offense level, serial-number adjustment, fleeing adjustment, and § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement
Criminal History Category VI and resulting advisory range of 292 to 365 months
What § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) requires: possession or use of a firearm in connection with another felony offense
Application note 14(C): enhancement applies even without a separate charge or conviction for the other felony
The importance of Cutbank’s failure to object to PSR factual statements about his conduct
The district court’s reliance on unobjected-to PSR facts to find the firearm was used in connection with another felony
The appellate court’s rejection of Cutbank’s argument that the enhancement conflicted with the parsimony principle of 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)
The relationship between the ACCA guideline calculation and the higher offense level produced by § 2K2.1-based adjustments under USSG § 4B1.4(b)
Gall and Rosales-Mireles: the need to correctly calculate the Guidelines before assessing reasonableness
Procedural reasonableness versus substantive reasonableness on appeal
The presumption of reasonableness for a within-Guidelines sentence in the Eighth Circuit
The district court’s consideration of the PSR, sentencing memoranda, and § 3553(a) factors
Aggravating facts supporting the 292-month sentence: extensive violent criminal history, domestic abuse, kidnapping-like confinement, assault, and injury to a police officer
Final disposition: no procedural error, no abuse of sentencing discretion, and affirmance of the 292-month sentence
